title: Spaghetti aglio, olio, e peperoncino
subtitle: Garlic, oil, and chilli on spaghetti
excerpt: Spaghetti tossed with thinly sliced garlic fried golden in olive oil, dried chilli flakes, and a fistful of flat-leaf parsley. The midnight pasta of Naples. Five ingredients, twenty minutes.
sourceNotes: Neapolitan tradition; documented in various forms throughout 20th-century Italian regional cookery. Cross-referenced with Elizabeth David, Italian Food (1954), which describes the simplicity of southern Italian garlic pasta.

content.text: Spaghetti aglio, olio, e peperoncino is the classic late-night pasta of southern Italy. The ingredients are spaghetti, garlic, olive oil, dried chilli, and parsley. Nothing else. The entire skill is in frying the garlic to exactly golden without letting it burn, and in building the emulsion that coats the pasta.
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Salt it generously (it should taste of the sea). Add {{pasta-dried}} spaghetti and cook 2 minutes less than the packet says.

While the pasta cooks, warm the olive oil in a wide pan over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook slowly until it turns pale gold at the edges, about 5 to 7 minutes. Watch it closely: golden is what you want, brown is bitter.
Add the chilli flakes and stir for 30 seconds. Take the pan off the heat.
Scoop out a large cup (about 200 ml) of pasta cooking water before draining. Drain the pasta.

Return the pan with the oil and garlic to medium heat. Add the pasta and about half the pasta water. Toss vigorously for 90 seconds, adding more pasta water as needed, until the sauce coats every strand and looks slightly creamy rather than oily.
Off the heat, add the parsley and toss again. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The garlic has burnt and tastes bitter
items.fix: Start over with fresh garlic and oil; bitter garlic cannot be rescued. Use the lowest possible heat and watch carefully.

items.symptom: The pasta is dry and clumping
items.cause: Not enough pasta water was used in the toss
items.fix: Add more pasta water, a tablespoon at a time, off the heat, and toss vigorously. The starch in the water emulsifies with the oil.

items.symptom: The oil has pooled at the bottom rather than coating the pasta
items.cause: The pasta water was not added or not tossed enough
items.fix: Add pasta water and toss the pasta continuously for a full 90 seconds. The tossing builds the emulsion.

items.symptom: The dish is not spicy enough
items.cause: Old chilli flakes that have lost their heat
items.fix: Use fresh chilli flakes or add a whole dried chilli to the oil alongside the garlic.

content.text: This is the pasta Neapolitans make when they come home late and the fridge is nearly empty. It demands almost nothing from the cook except the patience to fry the garlic without burning it. The combination of oil, starchy pasta water, and the heat of the pan creates a coating that is silky rather than greasy. Cheese is traditional in northern Italy but in Naples, where this belongs, it is usually left off.
